[Thinking]
**Offering study strategies**

The user is looking for general study advice, so I want to provide some actionable strategies, including techniques like active recall, spaced repetition, and practice tests. I'll also touch on the importance of environment, time management, note-taking, and specific exam tips, such as how to cope with anxiety and how to create a last-minute plan. It's all about being concise! If the user shares their subject or exam date, I can customize my suggestions further.
[/Thinking]

Good — here’s a practical, compact plan you can adapt for any exam. If you tell me the subject and how much time you have I can make it specific.

1) Organize and plan
- List what will be on the exam (topics, chapters, question types). If you don’t know, ask your teacher or use old exams/syllabus.
- Break the content into chunks and estimate how long each takes.
- Make a study schedule for every day until the exam. Prioritize high-weight or weak topics first.

2) Use effective study techniques
- Active recall: test yourself from memory (flashcards, closed-book summaries, practice problems). Don’t just reread.
- Spaced repetition: review material multiple times with increasing intervals (use apps like Anki or schedule review days).
- Practice testing: do past papers and timed practice questions. Grade them and review every mistake.
- Interleaving: mix related topics rather than studying one topic in a long block — improves transfer and retention.
- Teach/summarize: explain concepts aloud as if teaching someone else or write one-page summaries.

3) Note-taking and materials
- Make concise notes with key formulas, concepts, and example problems.
- Create one “cheat sheet” of essential formulas/concepts (even if you can’t bring it to the exam — making it is great review).
- Use diagrams, concept maps, and worked examples for problem-solving subjects.

4) Study sessions and environment
- Use focused sessions (Pomodoro: 25–50 minutes work, 5–10 minute break). After 3–4 sessions take a longer break.
- Minimize distractions (phone on Do Not Disturb, clean workspace).
- Alternate active work (problems, recall) with light review to avoid fatigue.

5) Practice under exam conditions
- Time yourself, stick to the allowed materials, simulate exam environment (quiet, no notes unless allowed).
- After each practice test, make an error log: why you missed, what to fix, then rework similar problems.

6) Health and mental prep
- Sleep: aim for 7–9 hours; sleep helps consolidation.
- Nutrition and hydration: eat balanced meals and drink water.
- Short exercise and relaxation techniques (deep breathing) to manage anxiety.
- Use brief mental warm-ups before the exam (review your cheat sheet or key formulas).

7) Last week and last 24–48 hours
- In the final week, switch from learning new material to consolidation and practice tests.
- Review your error log and high-yield summaries.
- In the last 24 hours: light review of core facts/formulas, rest, and plan logistics (what to bring, how to get there).

8) Tools and resources
- Flashcards (Anki, Quizlet)
- Note apps (Notion, OneNote) or paper notebooks
- Past papers, textbook problem sets, summary videos (Khan Academy, Crash Course)
- Study groups for explaining and testing each other (useful but ensure they stay focused)

If you tell me: the subject(s), exam date(s), how many hours per day you can study, and whether the exam is multiple-choice or problem-solving, I’ll make a tailored study schedule and a prioritized topic list.
